content.summary_of_the_paper:
- Paper studies the setting of model-free offline RL. A major challenge in this setting is the design of good conservative value/critic estimates necessary to prevent the policy from choosing OOD actions.
- This work proposes an alternative conservative critic (double conservative estimates; DCE) that relies on learning neural networks to approximate both the V and Q functions, which are coupled together through a SARSA style loss function. An expectile loss function is used to learn these functions instead of MSE, following IQL.
- The algorithm also considers an additional penalty term which simply minimizes the Q function in OOD actions chosen by current policy.
- Paper provides basic theoretical analysis to motivate the algorithm, and evaluates the practical algorithm on D4RL tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- There is limited novelty in the paper. Section 4.2 is not novel and this OOD penalty has been studied in the CQL paper. The use of expectile loss and SARSA style update was studied in the IQL paper. Overall, this paper looks like a direct combination of the two ideas.
- The results are only marginally better compared to prior work. Comparisons with model-based RL methods are lacking (e.g. MOReL, Trajectory Transformer etc)
- There are several typos throughout the paper (too many to list here) suggesting that it was written in a rush. I'd encourage the authors to thoroughly read the paper again and correct spelling and grammatical errors.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers offline RL where the goal is to find an optimal policy given a fixed dataset. One of the main problems in offline RL is OOD actions where they can negatively affect Q-estimates. To address this problem, this work proposes to combine two approaches to impose conservative estimates:  V-function (from implicit Q-learning paper) and Q-value penalty term (based on conseravitve Q-value papers). V-fucntion is there to reduce in-distribution action estimation and Q-penalty to control Q-values conservativim. To validate their approach, they run experiments on common tasks of D4RL benchmark and their method show promising results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- This paper shows good results.
- The proposed approach considers the right problem to address in offline learning which is OOD actions. 
-  This method is straightforward and easy to understand.

Weaknesses:

- Imprecise writing: While the paper is generally written well, there are some statements in the paper which are questionable. For instance, this paper  claims "Our algorithm does not require additional pre-training and maintains higher computational efficiency".  I am not entirely sure that is correct or I understood it correctly. Take CQL as an example, this paper even includes more training steps than CQL as this method requires training of V-function while CQL doesn't ( the same goes with section 5.4). Even If this refers to BC ( like BRAC), there are methods which don't clone CQL [1] or CDC [2]. Also, the paper has statements like "which can avoid the problem of the bellman equation".  It is not clear what is the problem of the bellman.

- Relation to previous work:
This paper reads like [2] especially the discussion about OOD actions and motivation about using Q-value penalty but yet not discussed in the paper. In addition, extra training in [2] is not issue if authors means BC by extra training,

- State-of-the-art:
This paper claims they have state-of-the-art results. Since that is the author's claim, methods like EDAC [3] have not been either discussed or cited in the paper.

- Hyper-parameters:
This paper has more hyper-parameters than other works and uses different one per environment, i.e. $\beta$, $\tau$ . More importantly, it seems it is critical to select the right set of hyper-parameters per author's experiments (Figure 2 and Figure 1) which is huge downside for this method.


Other comments:
- Eq 7 seems incorrect as there is no $a'$ in eq 7 ( Q-penalty term). if eq 7 is derivative of eq 6, there should be a' in it, right?

- Can you explain (and write down in the appendix )  how you get eq 8 from eq 7? Also explain how you derive the third term in eq  9 from the second term?

- Can you explain why your policy update doesn't need average loss in Eq 11? referring to this "In practice, policy loss of our algorithm does not require -\frac{1}{B}"

- Both policy and Q-value are parameterized by $\theta$.  Eq says both have the same parameters.   

[1]  Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.04779.pdf

[2]  Continuous Doubly Constrained Batch Reinforcement Learning https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.09225.pdf

[3] Uncertainty-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning with Diversified Q-Ensemble  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.01548.pdf
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is generally well written except for a few couple of important statements ( see my above comments). In terms of originality, this work is largely based on previous works.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The idea of the paper is simple and it seems to work. However, there are major issues like choice of specific hyper-parameters per environment, SOTA claim, similarity to previous works have. That said, I don't think this paper meets ICLR acceptance as it stands. But I will make the final recommendation after rebuttal. I'd like to hear their responses.    

------------------------

------UPDATE---------

After reading authors' responses and other reviews, I believe this paper needs major revision and not ready for ICLR. Hence, I'd recommend this paper to be rejected.

content.title: Reply to weaknesses and comments
content.comment:
### About pre-training and my description of problem of the bellman:
#### For pre-training, we mean algorithms that require additional agents (e.g. Fisher-BRC). At the same time, CQL needs to compute logsumexp and is, therefore, less efficient than us in terms of computational efficiency. Specifically, we compare the time of several algorithms executing in one epoch. "which can avoid the problem of the bellman equation" comes from my understanding of IQL. The specific contents are "Instead of estimating expectiles just with respect to the actions in the support of the data, it also incorporates stochasticity that comes from the environment dynamics $s^\prime\sim p(\cdot|s,a)$. Therefore, a large target value might not necessarily reflect the existence of a single action that achieves that value, but rather a "lucky" sample that happened to have transitioned into a good state."
### Relation to previous work:
#### I have added discussion of this paper in 4.2.
### About EDAC
#### EDAC outperforms ours on most MuJoCo tasks, but our method outperforms EDAC on some Adroit tasks. However, since EDAC requires many Q-nets (the paper shows that at least 10 Q-nets are needed to achieve that effect and in theory, this algorithm can improve performance by increasing the number of Q-net.), it is worse than our algorithm in terms of computational complexity and time. Specifically, using 50 critics(configuration of hopper) will cost over 100s on RTX3070, but our algorithm needs 12s.
### About parameters:
#### We set $\tau = 0.7$ like IQL, so we adjust the $\beta$ only. $\beta = 4$ usually gets a sub-optimal performance.
### comment 1:
#### In eq 7, we discuss the case where the action sampled by policy belongs to in-distribution, and we see this action as an action sampled by dataset. Therefore, we use "a" instead of "$a^\prime$" to avoid ambiguity.
### comment 2:
#### For eq 7, we set $\bigtriangledown L = 0$ to get eq 8. We use the iterative method to get eq 9.We add this in Appendix G. 
### comment 3:
#### We use SAC to update policy. I will replace that equation with an equivalent formula.
### cpmment 4:
#### I will revise this notation and thanks for your advice.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Double Conservative Estimation, which learns an in-distribution Value function and additionally applies a conservative Q-function objective to penalize OOD actions. DCE is compared to common offline RL algorithms on the D4RL benchmarks and shows improvement.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Proposes a method that combines effective elements of combatting value overestimation in offline RL and studies a well-motivated topic.
2. Comparison to sota offline RL algorithms on standard benchmarks and show improvement.

Weakness:
1. Some of the experiments are not well motivated. For example, it is unclear to me what the $\tau$ sweep in the beginning of Section 5 accomplishes; the corresponding Figure 1 is also not well labeled. Likewise, it would be helpful stating upfront what Section 5.1 is set out to accomplish. While the paper presents that the performance depends greatly on the value of $\beta$, is this desirable and how does this inform using the proposed algorithm in practice?

2. The proposed method is limited in novelty; it appears to be a simple combination of the core elements of IQL and CQL, namely in-distribution value function learning and conservative Q back-up. This is not in itself an issue if some deeper insight on how to best combine these two classes of approaches is provided, but that appears to be missing. 

3. The theoretical analysis is incorrect or improper. For one, depending on the scale of reward, the effect of beta in (8) can become arbitrarily small? It is also not clear to me how (8) is derived from (7). The performance analysis appears to be too conservative and not meaningful in practice. As such, this analysis section falls short of what you would expect for a theoretical analysis for Q-learning style offline RL algorithms.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The exposition is generally vague and confusing. From the introduction, it is hard to parse what's the proposed method is, and why it is well motivated. There are many places of jargon and colloquial language introduced without further qualification or explanation, such as "computational efficiency", "it is enough", and "valuation error of conservative estimation". The notation in (11) is also not standard, and the explanation about not having to account for $\frac{1}{|B|}$ is, in my opinion, common knowledge, and perhaps distracting in the main paper.

Novelty:
The novelty is fairly limited with respect to prior work. The first term in (6) is taken from IQL, whereas the second term comes from CQL. 

Grammatical errors:
"However, this means that IQL is too “conservatism” to discover the optimal action,"
"In this section, we will show our work, which aim is [...]"

Questions:
1. What is the hat notation in (4)?
2. (5) is a biased estimate due to the double sampling issue (Baird, 1995); this should be mentioned somewhere. 
3. How does (8) follow from (7)?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while the idea in the paper warrants some careful study as it combines some most commonly used techniques in offline RL, this paper's execution falls short of meeting the bar of ICLR due to its lack of rigor and substance in terms of both theory and experimentation. Furthermore, the paper's exposition and clarity can also be greatly improved.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a new offline RL algorithm -- DCE -- that learns a conservative Q-function by combining two approaches: (1) learn a conservative V-function using a quantile loss, and (2) add a penalty over OOD Q-values in the objective. The authors show that the learned Q-function lower-bounds the true one. Finally, the authors empirically evaluate DCE against related baselines, such as CQL and IQL, and show that DCE outperforms existing offline RL algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
(1) The empirical performance of DCE over CQL, IQL is impressive.
(2) The paper is well-written and the approach is described clearly. 

Weaknesses:
(1) The actual algorithm simply combines the approaches of CQL and IQL into a single algorithm, which can be viewed as weak from a novelty standpoint.
(2) The algorithm has multiple tunable parameters, more so than competing offline RL algorithms, that seem to drastically affect performance (particularly \tau and \beta). 
(3) The choice of policy loss (using SAC instead of AWR) seems a bit arbitrary. It would be helpful if the authors discussed why this choice was made.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The work is well-written and its proposed algorithm is clearly explained. I do have issues with the novelty, as it simply combines the key ideas of two well-known offline RL algorithms CQL and IQL.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper proposes a new algorithm that achieves impressive results against existing state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms. I do think that the algorithm itself lacks novelty, as it takes the objective for learning V-functions in IQL and combines it with the objective for learning Q-functions in CQL. I also think that some choices in the algorithm design, specifically in policy learning (using SAC instead of AWR), are a bit arbitrary and can be better motivated. However, due to the good empirical performance, I still recommend that the paper be accepted.
